title: Tuga WH6 vs Tuga W10: Windows Handheld or 10 Inch Tablet?
description: Tuga WH6 (Windows handheld, £699) or Tuga W10 (10.1 inch Windows tablet, £649)? £50 apart, and the bigger one is cheaper. Which to buy, and when each fits.
summary: £50 apart and the bigger one is cheaper: the W10 is a 10.1 inch Windows 11 Pro tablet with Ethernet and HDMI, the WH6 a 470g Windows 11 handheld with 4G LTE.
lede: For anyone who needs Windows on site and is torn between a handheld and a full-size tablet. The short answer: buy the Tuga W10 and keep £50 if the work happens on a screen, at a panel or on a desk, and pay the extra for the Tuga WH6 only if the device has to be carried and used in one hand all day.
verdict: Shape decides this one, and the bigger device is the cheaper one. The Tuga W10 costs £649 and the Tuga WH6 costs £699, so the handheld is £50 more. Both run Windows 11 with 8GB of RAM and 128GB of storage, and both are rated IP65. For £50 less, the W10 gives you a 10.1 inch 1280 x 800 screen against 6.5 inches at 720 x 1600, an Intel N100 (up to 3.4GHz) against a Celeron N5100 (up to 2.8GHz), a 5000mAh battery against 4000mAh, and RJ45 Ethernet and HDMI ports the WH6 does not list. If the job is forms, drawings, spreadsheets, or a program that talks to a panel over a cable, the W10 is the better buy as well as the cheaper one.

The extra £50 buys a device you can carry and use in one hand all day. The WH6 weighs 470g against 1197g for the W10, a difference of 727g, and it fits the Belt Holster (£22). It also has 4G LTE and GPS + GLONASS built in, where the W10 lists 4G LTE and GPS as options, and it lists MIL-STD-810H, a 1.5 metre drop spec and a -20°C to 60°C operating range, none of which the W10 lists. The trade-off is the screen: at 6.5 inches it is for scanning, ticking and signing off, not for reading a drawing. If the device stays in a holster and comes out for a stock check or an instrument reading in a Windows program you already use, the WH6 is worth the £50.

Two things to check before you order either. The WH6 runs Windows 11 IoT and the W10 Windows 11 Pro, so if a software provider specifies an edition, ask them which they support, and in both cases check that the programs you rely on run on the device rather than assuming they will. Both come in scanner versions sold from the same product page as the standard model: the WH6 with Barcode Scanner is £779 and the W10 with 2D Scanner is £729, both £80 over the standard model, so the gap stays at £50. For warehouse and stock work where your software forces Windows, the logistics page covers the WH6 with scanner; for engineers who plug into equipment and work on a bigger screen, our guide to tablets for field engineers covers the W10 and where it sits against the W8.
chooseA: The device lives in a holster or a pocket and is used in one hand: the WH6 is a 6.5 inch handheld at 470g, 727g lighter than the W10, and fits the Belt Holster (£22).
You need a mobile connection and a position fix as standard: 4G LTE and GPS + GLONASS are built into the WH6, where the W10 lists 4G LTE and GPS as options.
You want listed toughness figures: the WH6 lists MIL-STD-810H, a 1.5 metre drop spec and a -20°C to 60°C operating range, and the W10 lists none of the three.
You photograph jobs on the device: the WH6's rear camera is 8MP autofocus against 5MP on the W10.
Scanning is the job rather than part of it: the WH6 with Barcode Scanner (£779) is a handheld, where the W10 with 2D Scanner (£729) is a 10.1 inch tablet.
chooseB: The work happens on the screen: forms, drawings, spreadsheets and desktop software are easier on 10.1 inches at 1280 x 800 than on 6.5 inches, and you keep £50.
You plug into panels, plant or network gear with a cable: the W10 has RJ45 Ethernet and HDMI as well as the USB-C and USB-A ports both devices have.
It lives on a desk or a dashboard: the W10 fits the Charging Dock (£49.99) and the Vehicle Mounting Dock (£109), and a hand strap is in the box.
You want a higher-clocked processor and a larger battery: an Intel N100 (up to 3.4GHz) against a Celeron N5100 (up to 2.8GHz), and a removable 5000mAh battery against 4000mAh.
You want cover beyond 12 months: the paid 3-Year Warranty (£79) is offered on the W10 and not on the WH6.

faq.q: Is the Tuga WH6 worth £50 more than the Tuga W10?
faq.a: Only if you need the shape. The WH6 costs £699 and the W10 £649, and the W10 is the bigger device with a higher-clocked processor, more ports and the larger removable battery, so the £50 buys a smaller, lighter handheld with 4G LTE and GPS built in, not more computer. If the device is mostly used on a lap or a desk while you read, at a panel, in a dock or on a dashboard, the Tuga W10 gives you more for less. If it spends its day in a holster and comes out for a scan, a signature or a reading, the Tuga WH6 justifies the difference. Both include 12 months of warranty; the paid 3-Year Warranty (£79) is offered on the W10 only, and business fleets of ten or more W10s can ask about the quote-only Total Care plan.

faq.q: Which one should I buy for barcode scanning?
faq.a: The handheld if scanning is the main job, the W10 if scanning is part of a bigger task at a bench or desk. Both come in a scanner version, sold from the same product page as the standard model and £80 over it: the Tuga WH6 with Barcode Scanner is £779 and the Tuga W10 with 2D Scanner is £729. The WH6 version lists an integrated 2D scanner that reads all major barcode formats, and the Belt Holster (£22) gives it somewhere to go between scans. The W10 version lists a Newland 2D scan engine that reads 1D barcodes plus QR, PDF417, Aztec and MaxiCode, with a UHF RFID reader as a further option, and the screen and Ethernet port suit stock counts typed into a system. Our guide to built-in barcode scanners covers when the extra £80 pays off at all.

faq.q: Do both have removable batteries, and how do they compare?
faq.a: Yes, both list a removable battery: 5000mAh in the W10 and 4000mAh in the WH6, so the tablet starts the day with more capacity, and a removable battery means a charged spare can be swapped in where you have one. Spare batteries are not listed with the accessories, so check with us via the contact page before you plan around one. For charging in place, the WH6 Charging Cradle is £79, the Charging Dock for the W10 is £49.99, and the 12V DC Car Charger (£26) fits either, all on the accessories page. The WH6 lists an operating range of -20°C to 60°C and the W10 lists no operating temperature, so if the device lives in an unheated van through winter, the WH6 is the one with a listed figure. Our guide to rugged tablets in winter explains what the cold does to either battery.

faq.q: Do they run the same Windows software?
faq.a: Not necessarily, so check. Both have 8GB of RAM and 128GB of storage, but the processors differ, an Intel N100 (up to 3.4GHz) in the W10 and an Intel Celeron N5100 (up to 2.8GHz) in the WH6, and so does the edition: the WH6 runs Windows 11 IoT and the W10 Windows 11 Pro. Ask your software provider which Windows editions they support, and check that the specific programs you rely on run on the device before you order rather than assuming they will. Software that talks to equipment over a network cable is the W10's case, since only the W10 lists an RJ45 Ethernet port; a program that needs the device's own mobile connection is simpler on the WH6, which has 4G LTE built in where the W10 lists it as an option. If you want Windows on 8 inches instead, the Tuga W8 at £629 is the 8 inch Windows 11 Pro tablet in the range, and it is cheaper than either.
